lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you learnt 'first in, first out'. What does it mean in a kitchen? (Use the older food first.) Today: how food gets from the farm to your fork.
Food is grown or reared. Arable farms grow crops such as wheat and potatoes; livestock farms raise animals for milk, eggs and meat. Fish are caught at sea or farmed.

Intensive farming gets a lot of food from a little land, using machines, fertilisers and sprays. Organic farming limits chemicals and gives animals more space, but usually needs more land. Both have trade-offs.
Primary processing makes a raw food ready to use, like milling wheat into flour. Secondary processing makes new products from it, like baking flour into bread.
Food is kept safe for longer. Pasteurising heats milk to 72 °C for 15 seconds to kill harmful bacteria. Canning, freezing, drying and chilling slow down the microbes that spoil food.
Food miles count how far food travels; food flown by air has a far bigger footprint than food shipped by sea. But often what a food is matters more: beef's footprint is about 100 times that of peas.

lesson.text: Seasonal food grows at its natural time, so it needs less heating and flying: UK strawberries in summer, apples in autumn. Sustainable choices: less waste, more plants, and fair pay for farmers.
Try it in the world: read the labels at home and find where three foods were grown. In LIFE, The Kitchen keeps food safe, raw and cooked apart, and cooks a meal. Next: circular design.

exercises.prompt: An arable farm or a livestock farm?
exercises.hint: Is it a crop that grows, or an animal that is raised?
exercises.explain: Arable: wheat, potatoes, barley. Livestock: dairy cows and hens.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is primary processing?
exercises.hint: Primary processing gets a raw food ready to use.
exercises.explain: Milling turns raw wheat into flour, ready to use; the others make new products from flour.

exercises.prompt: Pasteurising milk heats it to kill harmful bacteria.
exercises.hint: Think of the temperature and time.
exercises.explain: True: heating milk to 72 °C for 15 seconds kills harmful bacteria but keeps the milk tasting fresh.

exercises.hint: Grow, gather, process, make, then deliver.
exercises.explain: Wheat grows, is harvested, milled into flour, baked into bread and delivered.

exercises.prompt: Which food on the chart has the biggest footprint for each kilogram?

picture.name: kg of gases per kg of food

exercises.explain: Beef's bar reaches about 100 kg of gases per kg, the tallest by far.

exercises.prompt: Which way of moving food usually gives the biggest footprint?
exercises.hint: Planes burn a lot of fuel for every kilogram they carry.
exercises.explain: Air freight has a far bigger footprint for each kilogram and kilometre than ships or trains.

exercises.prompt: Match each food to a product made from it (secondary processing).
exercises.hint: What new product is made from each one?
exercises.explain: Flour makes bread, milk makes cheese, potatoes make crisps, and fruit makes jam.

exercises.prompt: Chicken gives off about 10 kg of greenhouse gases per kg. About how much for 0.5 kg?
exercises.hint: Multiply the footprint for 1 kg by the kilograms.

exercises.prompt: Organic farming usually needs more land than intensive farming for the same food.
exercises.hint: Think about fewer fertilisers and more space for animals.
exercises.explain: True: with fewer chemicals and more space, each field usually produces less, so more land is needed.

exercises.prompt: More like intensive farming, or organic?
exercises.hint: Which aims for the most food per field, and which limits chemicals?
exercises.explain: Intensive: machines, sprays, fertilisers, the most per field. Organic: fewer sprays, more space for animals.

exercises.prompt: Which is in season in the UK in summer?
exercises.hint: Look at the summer row of the table.
exercises.explain: Strawberries ripen in the UK summer; the others are autumn and winter crops.

exercises.prompt: Swapping 0.25 kg of beef (about 100 kg of gases per kg) for peas (about 1 kg) saves how many kg?
exercises.hint: Find the saving for 1 kg, then multiply by 0.25.

exercises.prompt: Why can tomatoes grown in a heated greenhouse nearby have a bigger footprint than ones shipped from abroad?
choices: heating the greenhouse uses a lot of energy
exercises.hint: Count all the energy, not only the miles.
exercises.explain: Heating a greenhouse through a cold season can use more energy than shipping sun-grown tomatoes: food miles are only part of the story.

exercises.prompt: A meal has 0.2 kg of chicken (about 10 kg of gases per kg) and 0.1 kg of cheese (about 24). About how many kg of gases in all?
exercises.hint: Work out each food's footprint, then add.

exercises.prompt: Food miles alone tell you a food's whole footprint.
exercises.hint: Think of what happens on the farm, not only on the journey.
exercises.explain: False: farming often makes most of the footprint, so what a food is can matter more than how far it went.

exercises.hint: Farm, keep it cold, make it safe, make the product, sell.
exercises.explain: Milking, chilling, pasteurising (primary), cheese-making (secondary), then selling.
